note.explanation: Group 17 elements are halogens. They have seven outer-shell electrons and tend to gain one electron. Their reactivity and oxidising power decrease down the group, while their atomic radii and the melting and boiling points increase.
examples: Chlorine displaces bromine from sodium bromide: Cl₂ + 2NaBr → 2NaCl + Br₂.
Hydrogen bromide is less thermally stable than hydrogen chloride: HCl > HBr in thermal stability.
note.checkAnswer: Chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent, so it gains electrons and displaces bromine from bromide ions.
note.simple: Halogens usually gain one electron. The halogens near the top of the group gain it more easily, so they are more reactive.
note.checkQuestion: Which is the stronger oxidising agent, chlorine or bromine, and why?
note.title: Group 17: Halogens
steps: Identify which halogen is higher in Group 17.
The higher halogen has greater oxidising power.
It can displace a lower halogen from a solution of its halide.
note.answer: Chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent. It can displace bromine from a bromide solution.

mcqs.stem: Which halogen has the lowest reactivity?
rationales: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen, not the least.
Chlorine is more reactive than bromine and iodine.
Bromine is more reactive than iodine.
Iodine is lowest in the group and has the least reactivity.

mcqs.stem: Which order shows the oxidising power of these halogens from greatest to least?
rationales: Oxidising power decreases down the group, giving this order.
This reverses the order given by the decrease down the group.
Bromine is not a stronger oxidising agent than chlorine.
Their oxidising powers are not equal.

mcqs.stem: Which halogen can displace bromide ions from sodium bromide solution?
rationales: Iodine is less powerful as an oxidising agent than bromine and cannot displace it.
Bromine cannot displace itself from its own halide.
Chlorine has greater oxidising power than bromine and displaces it.
Fluorine is more reactive, but the textbook displacement examples use chlorine; chlorine is the correct choice among the listed examples for bromide displacement.

mcqs.stem: Which halogen is a shiny grey solid that forms dark purple vapour when warmed?
rationales: Fluorine is a pale yellow gas.
Chlorine is a yellowish green gas.
Bromine is a fuming red-brown liquid.
Iodine is a shiny grey solid that forms dark purple vapour when warmed.

mcqs.stem: Which hydrogen halide has the highest thermal stability?
rationales: HF has the highest thermal stability in the order HF > HCl > HBr > HI.
HCl is thermally stable, but less so than HF.
HBr is less thermally stable than HCl.
HI has the lowest thermal stability in the order.

mcqs.stem: Which hydrogen halide is described in the textbook as a liquid at ordinary temperature?
rationales: Hydrogen fluoride is the exception and is described as a liquid.
Hydrogen chloride is not the stated exception.
Hydrogen bromide is not the stated exception.
Hydrogen iodide is not the stated exception.

options: They do not take part in electron transfer.

rationales: A chlorine atom gains one electron to form Cl⁻.
Losing an electron would not form a chloride ion.
Chlorine gains one, not two, electrons to form Cl⁻.
Chlorine accepts an electron in this process.

options: Atomic radii decrease down the group.
Melting and boiling points increase down the group.
Oxidising power increases down the group.

rationales: Atomic radii increase, rather than decrease, down the group.
The textbook states that melting and boiling points increase down the group.

written.text: How do halogens react with water?
written.finalAnswer: Chlorine reacts with water to form hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid; hypochlorous acid helps sterilize the water.

rubric.why: Naming the halogen reaction identifies what happens to water treated with chlorine.
rubric.description: State that chlorine reacts with water.
rubric.how: Write that chlorine dissolves and reacts with water.

rubric.why: The products explain the chemical change and the sterilising effect.
rubric.description: Name the products and the sterilising substance.
rubric.how: Give hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid, noting that hypochlorous acid helps sterilize water.

modelAnswer: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO
Chlorine reacts with water to form hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid.
Hypochlorous acid helps sterilize the water.

written.text: Q9.2. Predict the reactivity of potassium towards halogens.
written.finalAnswer: Potassium reacts readily with halogens to form ionic metal halides, because potassium loses one electron and a halogen gains one electron.

rubric.why: The prediction of a vigorous reaction is the central answer.
rubric.description: Predict that potassium reacts readily with halogens.
rubric.how: State that potassium is highly reactive towards halogens.

rubric.why: Electron transfer explains the formation of a metal halide.
rubric.description: Explain electron transfer and formation of a halide.
rubric.how: State that potassium loses one electron, the halogen gains it, and an ionic halide forms.

modelAnswer: Potassium reacts readily with halogens.
Potassium loses one electron and a halogen atom gains one electron.
Ionic metal halides are formed.

written.text:
Q9.3. In the following reaction, chlorine acts as an oxidising agent. Which is the reducing agent?

Cl₂(aq) + 2NaBr(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + Br₂(g)
written.finalAnswer: Sodium bromide (NaBr), specifically the bromide ions, is the reducing agent.

rubric.why: The question asks for the reducing agent in the given reaction.
rubric.description: Identify sodium bromide as the reducing agent.
rubric.how: Name NaBr, or specify its bromide ions.

rubric.why: The reducing agent loses electrons while reducing the other substance.
rubric.description: Explain that bromide ions lose electrons.
rubric.how: Show or state that Br⁻ ions lose electrons to form Br₂.

modelAnswer: Br⁻ ions lose electrons to form Br₂.
Therefore, NaBr (the bromide ions) is the reducing agent.

written.text: Q9.4. Why does iodine exist in the solid state at room temperature?
written.finalAnswer: Iodine molecules are large and attract each other strongly, so iodine has a relatively high melting point and is solid at room temperature.

rubric.why: The stronger attractions between larger halogen molecules explain the increase in melting point.
rubric.description: Link iodine's larger molecules to stronger attractions.
rubric.how: State that iodine molecules are large and attract one another strongly.

rubric.why: This connects the molecular explanation to iodine's physical state.
rubric.description: Conclude that iodine is solid at room temperature.
rubric.how: State that iodine's melting point is high enough for it to be solid at room temperature.

modelAnswer: Iodine molecules are large and attract one another strongly.
This gives iodine a relatively high melting point.
Therefore, iodine is solid at room temperature.

written.text: Q9.6. Compare the reactivity of chlorine and bromine as an oxidising agent.
written.finalAnswer: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine: Cl₂ > Br₂. Chlorine accepts electrons more readily and can displace bromide ions from solution.

rubric.why: The relative order is the direct comparison requested.
rubric.description: State that chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent.
rubric.how: Give Cl₂ > Br₂ or state that chlorine is stronger than bromine.

rubric.why: The electron gain or displacement explains the oxidising action.
rubric.description: Give a reason for chlorine's greater oxidising power.
rubric.how: Explain that chlorine accepts electrons more readily or displaces bromide ions.

modelAnswer: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine.
Cl₂ > Br₂
Chlorine accepts electrons more readily and can displace bromide ions from solution.

written.text: Q9.7. Which element is the most reactive and which is the least reactive among halogens? Give two reasons to explain your answer.
written.finalAnswer: Fluorine is the most reactive and iodine is the least reactive. Down the group, atomic size increases and the tendency to accept an electron decreases; therefore, reactivity decreases.

rubric.why: The answer must correctly identify the most reactive halogen.
rubric.description: Name fluorine as the most reactive.
rubric.how: State that fluorine is the most reactive halogen.

rubric.why: The answer must correctly identify the least reactive halogen.
rubric.description: Name iodine as the least reactive.
rubric.how: State that iodine is the least reactive halogen.

rubric.why: Increasing atomic size is one textbook reason for the downward trend.
rubric.description: Give the increase in atomic size down the group.
rubric.how: State that atomic size or atomic radius increases down Group 17.

rubric.why: The decreasing tendency to accept an electron explains the decreasing reactivity.
rubric.description: Give the decrease in tendency to accept an electron.
rubric.how: State that the tendency to accept an electron decreases down the group.

modelAnswer: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen.
Iodine is the least reactive halogen.
Atomic size increases down the group.
The tendency to accept an electron decreases down the group, so reactivity decreases.

written.text: Q9.2. Why do the chemical reactivities of alkali metals increase down the group whereas they decrease down the group in case of halogens?
written.finalAnswer: Alkali metals become more reactive down the group because their outer electron is farther from the nucleus and is lost more easily. Halogens become less reactive because atomic size increases down the group and their tendency to accept an electron decreases.

rubric.why: This states the first trend that the question asks the student to explain.
rubric.description: State that alkali-metal reactivity increases down the group.
rubric.how: Give the direction of the alkali-metal trend correctly.

rubric.why: Losing the outer electron more easily explains the metal trend.
rubric.description: Explain why alkali metals become more reactive.
rubric.how: State that the outer electron is lost more easily down the group.

rubric.why: This states the opposite trend for halogens.
rubric.description: State that halogen reactivity decreases down the group.
rubric.how: Give the direction of the halogen trend correctly.

rubric.why: The change in electron acceptance explains why halogens become less reactive.
rubric.description: Explain the halogen trend using size and electron acceptance.
rubric.how: State that increasing atomic size makes the tendency to accept an electron decrease.

modelAnswer: Alkali-metal reactivity increases down the group.
Their outer electron is farther from the nucleus and is lost more easily.
Halogen reactivity decreases down the group.
Atomic size increases and the tendency to accept an electron decreases.

written.text: Q9.4. Both alkali metals and halogens are very reactive elements with roles opposite to each other. Explain.
written.finalAnswer: Alkali metals lose one electron to form positive ions, so they act as reducing agents. Halogens gain one electron to form negative ions, so they act as oxidising agents. They react together to form ionic metal halides.

rubric.why: Electron loss gives the alkali metal its opposite role in electron transfer.
rubric.description: State that alkali metals lose an electron.
rubric.how: Explain that an alkali-metal atom forms a positive ion by losing one electron.

rubric.why: Electron gain gives the halogen its opposite role.
rubric.description: State that halogens gain or accept an electron.
rubric.how: Explain that a halogen atom forms a negative ion by gaining one electron.

rubric.why: The agent roles connect electron transfer to oxidation and reduction.
rubric.description: Identify the agents correctly.
rubric.how: Call the electron-losing metal a reducing agent and the electron-accepting halogen an oxidising agent.

rubric.why: The product shows the result of their opposite electron-transfer roles.
rubric.description: State the product formed when they react.
rubric.how: Name the ionic metal halide formed.

modelAnswer: An alkali metal loses one electron and forms a positive ion.
A halogen gains one electron and forms a negative ion.
The alkali metal acts as a reducing agent and the halogen acts as an oxidising agent.
They react to form ionic metal halides.

written.text: Q9.5. Why hydrogen bromide is thermally unstable as compared to hydrogen chloride?
written.finalAnswer: The H–Br bond is longer and weaker than the H–Cl bond because bromine is larger than chlorine. Less heat energy is needed to break the H–Br bond, so hydrogen bromide is less thermally stable.

rubric.why: The larger bromine atom explains the increase in bond length.
rubric.description: Compare the sizes of bromine and chlorine.
rubric.how: State that bromine is larger than chlorine.

rubric.why: The longer bond is a key link in the textbook explanation.
rubric.description: State that the hydrogen–bromine bond is longer.
rubric.how: Compare the H–Br bond length with the H–Cl bond length.

rubric.why: A weaker bond requires less energy to break.
rubric.description: State that the H–Br bond is weaker.
rubric.how: Explain that the longer H–Br bond is weaker than the H–Cl bond.

rubric.why: This links bond strength to thermal stability and gives the conclusion.
rubric.description: Conclude that hydrogen bromide is less thermally stable.
rubric.how: State that less heat is needed to break H–Br, so HBr is less thermally stable.

modelAnswer: Bromine is larger than chlorine, so the H–Br bond is longer than the H–Cl bond.
The H–Br bond is weaker.
Less heat energy is needed to break the H–Br bond.
Therefore, hydrogen bromide is less thermally stable than hydrogen chloride.

examTips: This section can appear as short-answer questions asking for a trend, a colour or physical state, or the role of an oxidising or reducing agent.
For a displacement reaction, compare the halogens' oxidising power first: Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. A stronger halogen displaces a weaker halogen from its halide.
For questions about trends, state the trend and then give the reason: atomic size increases down the group, while the tendency to accept an electron decreases.
For thermal stability, connect the increasing bond length down the group to weaker bonds, less energy needed to break them, and lower thermal stability.

explain.title: Outer electrons and reactivity
explain.body: Group 17 elements have seven electrons in their outermost shells (ns², np⁵). They tend to accept one electron and form negative ions. Their reactivity decreases down the group because atomic size increases and the tendency to accept an electron decreases.

explain.title: Physical properties down the group
explain.body: Atomic radii, melting points and boiling points increase down the group. Larger molecules attract each other more strongly. Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a fuming red-brown liquid, and iodine is a shiny grey solid that forms dark purple vapour when warmed.

explain.title: Oxidation, reduction and displacement
explain.body: Oxidation is a process in which an electron is lost. The substance which loses an electron is called a reducing agent. Reduction is a process in which an electron is gained and the substance which accepts the electron is called an oxidizing agent. Halogens are oxidising agents, and their oxidising power decreases in the order Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. A stronger halogen can displace a weaker halogen from its compound.

explain.title: Hydrogen halides
explain.body: Halogens react with hydrogen to give hydrogen halides: H₂ + X₂ → 2HX. Bond length increases down the group, so the bond gets weaker and needs less heat energy to break. Therefore, thermal stability decreases in the order HF > HCl > HBr > HI.

mistakes: Do not reverse the trends: halogen reactivity and oxidising power decrease down Group 17.
Do not confuse oxidation with reduction: oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain of electrons.
Do not say that the weaker halogen displaces the stronger one. The stronger oxidising halogen does the displacement.
When explaining hydrogen-halide stability, include the full chain: larger halogen atom, longer and weaker bond, less energy to break it, lower thermal stability.
Use the exact order Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ for oxidising power and HF > HCl > HBr > HI for thermal stability.
